name: Gurmukhi
signature: A headline runs along the top of most letters, as in Devanagari, but the letters are rounder and simpler, with no conjunct stacks; three vowel bearers (ੳ ਅ ੲ) carry the independent vowels.
combination: A consonant carries an inherent vowel a (ਕ = ka). A vowel sign replaces it (ਨ + ਾ → ਨਾ = nā); ਿ is written in front of the consonant it follows in speech. Vowels with no consonant ride on a bearer (ਅ + ਾ → ਆ ā). Bindi and tippi nasalize a vowel, addak doubles the next consonant, and the dot below (਼) marks borrowed sounds (ਸ਼ sha). A headline runs along the top of a word, joining its letters.
notes: The Punjabi track's own inventory: exactly the letters, signs and digits its lessons read (33 letters, 14 signs, 4 digits), each `sound` taken from that letter's own lesson romanization. It is not the whole alphabet (ੳ ੲ ਙ ਞ ਢ ਯ, the other six digits and the other nukta letters are not yet read), so `complete` is false. Stroke order is source-gated: only rows with `penLifts` and `strokeOrderSource` carry a cited order, from the Apache-2.0 tracing lesson of GNPS's Gurmukhi Sikho app (order, start, direction and lifts only; no checkpoint is copied), with Omniglot copyists' counts and shares as corroboration. Rows without them are recognition-only: `strokeOrder: []` means NOT VERIFIED, never none. The vowel signs, bindi, tippi, addak, halant and the dot below have no stroke-order source yet, so they stay undrawn; ਝ and ਧ, which the source covers, are left for a later batch because no lesson would print them yet.

strokeOrderSource.citation: GNPS, Gurmukhi Sikho (GNPS Learning Hub), Alphabet Tracing lesson, ਅ (airhaa) checkpoints, strokes 1–2 (lib/data/lessons/lesson_tracing.dart line 62, commit de1e560; Apache-2.0)
strokeOrderSource.variation: GNPS's children's Punjabi app (Apache-2.0; developer CodeManX) has a tracing lesson whose checkpoints the developer entered over the Noto Sans Gurmukhi letter, one list per pen-down stroke, and whose trace widget makes the child reach them in order. It writes ਅ in two pen-down strokes. The first starts at the top left, runs right along the left part of the bar and turns down, then turns clockwise through about two full turns as it crosses the letter, ending where the body meets the stem; the second starts at the top right, runs left along the bar's right part and turns down the stem to its foot. In the bundled Noto Sans Gurmukhi outline this letter's top bar is split, with a gap above the body, and the source draws no separate headline: the first stroke opens along the bar's left part and the last stroke opens by running right to left along its right part before turning down the stem. The outline and the source agree, so there is no headline stroke to place first or last. The outline prints both loops as solid tails, so the path loops clockwise inside each. Omniglot (Lake, Salakhutdinov & Tenenbaum, Science 350:1332, 2015; https://github.com/brendenlake/omniglot, MIT licence) holds 20 drawings of ਅ, each by a different non-native copyist; only counts and shares are cited. 65% (13 of 20) draw it in two strokes, the source's count and their most common one. For the first stroke of the body, 90% (18 of 20) start in the same part of the letter as the source and 55% (11 of 20) set off in the same direction, within 45 degrees. Only the order, the start, the direction and the lifts are taken from the source; no checkpoint coordinate is copied, and the path is fitted to the bundled Noto Sans Gurmukhi outline. Handwriting varies by writer.

strokeOrderSource.citation: GNPS, Gurmukhi Sikho (GNPS Learning Hub), Alphabet Tracing lesson, ੜ (rhaarhaa) checkpoints, strokes 1–3 (lib/data/lessons/lesson_tracing.dart line 1108, commit de1e560; Apache-2.0)
strokeOrderSource.variation: GNPS's children's Punjabi app (Apache-2.0; developer CodeManX) has a tracing lesson whose checkpoints the developer entered over the Noto Sans Gurmukhi letter, one list per pen-down stroke, and whose trace widget makes the child reach them in order. It writes ੜ in three pen-down strokes: the headline from left to right; then from the top right down to the left, clockwise round the knob and the right side, and left along the base to the bottom left; then the short right leg, down to the right. The headline first is the source's teaching order. Fluent writers are often described as adding the headline last (Alfaazo's general guidance on Gurmukhi; native Devanagari writers do so in HP Labs India's pen data), so the path shows how this lesson teaches the letter, not how every fluent hand writes it. The outline prints the knob as a solid teardrop, so the path loops clockwise inside it. Omniglot (Lake, Salakhutdinov & Tenenbaum, Science 350:1332, 2015; https://github.com/brendenlake/omniglot, MIT licence) holds 20 drawings of ੜ, each by a different non-native copyist; only counts and shares are cited. 65% (13 of 20) draw it in three strokes, the source's count and their most common one. For the first stroke of the body, 70% (14 of 20) start in the same part of the letter as the source and 85% (17 of 20) set off in the same direction, within 45 degrees. Only the order, the start, the direction and the lifts are taken from the source; no checkpoint coordinate is copied, and the path is fitted to the bundled Noto Sans Gurmukhi outline. Handwriting varies by writer.

marks.attachesAs: kanna: an upright stroke standing to the right of its consonant, hanging from the headline
sihari: an upright with a hook over the top, written to the LEFT of its consonant though spoken after it
bihari: an upright with a hook over the top, written to the right of its consonant
aunkar: a small hook hanging under its consonant
dulainkar: a double hook hanging under its consonant
lavan: one slanting stroke above the headline
dulavan: two slanting strokes above the headline
hora: a curl above the headline
kanaura: a curl and a slanting stroke above the headline
bindi: a dot above the headline, to the right, that sends the vowel through the nose
tippi: a small open curve above the headline that nasalizes the vowel
addak: a small crescent above the headline before the consonant it doubles
halant (pairin): marks a consonant written under or beside the next with no vowel of its own
pairin bindi: one dot under a letter, making a sound borrowed from Persian or English (ਸ + ਼ → ਸ਼ sha, ਫ + ਼ → ਫ਼ fa)
